  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
The rain had been falling in sheets against the windshield when Tasha’s phone finally connected to her brother Marcus, his voice crackling as he assured her he was fine. By the time the highway patrol bulletin came through on the local band, the details were already etched into her mind: a hydroplaned sedan, a chain-reaction collision, a twisted cab that matched the description of the truck she had insisted he take. When she arrived at the hospital, the smell of burnt rubber was still faint on her jacket from the tow yard. She had come to believe that if she had only driven him to the station herself, the steering wheel would still be intact. The self-blame settled into her bones like silt. She would never forgive herself for not doing more to stop what happened, and the conviction that she failed to protect the person who depended on her most felt like ballast in her chest. She was certain that the event happened because of the way she acted, that her hesitation and her misplaced confidence had sealed his fate. Over the following weeks, the days blurred into vigilance and withdrawal. She delayed sleep, staying up until very late as if exhaustion could outpace the memories, though the silence only gave her room to dwell on how the event could have been prevented. The compensation arrived in sudden trips to the store, where she would spend money impulsively to distract or comfort herself, buying items she did not need just to feel the sharp cut of the credit card. Her husband noticed the tension coiling in her shoulders, the way she flinched when the evening news shifted to traffic updates. She found herself unable to tolerate crash discussions, her jaw tightening and her chest constricting whenever the topic surfaced in her neighborhood group chats. What frightened her most was having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame flooding her without warning, and she began to isolate from community gatherings to keep her reactions contained. When she returned to work on the commercial fishing vessel, the deck offered little refuge. The VHF radio scanned constantly for weather shifts, and one morning, a dispatcher’s clipped voice reported a car hit by accident on the interstate near their hometown. Tasha dropped her mesh crates, her breath hitching as her pulse hammered against her ribs. She had strong physical reactions when something reminded her of the stressful experience—her hands trembled, her stomach turned, and a hot flush spread up her neck. When she later snapped at a deckhand over a misread winch cable, the shout echoed over the diesel engines. The irritability that fueled her angry outbursts or acting aggressively felt like a crack in her foundation, yet she kept working, unable to admit the past had taken root in her daily routine. Now, as November approached, the calendar on the galley bulkhead marked the anniversary of the event. The date carried a weight that made familiar tasks feel impossible. She had tried to push through the shift, but the compulsion to delay sleep had deepened into a habit she could not break. Her husband gently suggested counseling, and the words finally unspooled in her throat. She was most afraid that the memories would never settle, that the guilt would continue to dictate her choices, but she was also hoping for a space where she could finally stop counting the seconds until midnight. She packed her bag that evening, stepping into a room where she could name what happened without the deck under her feet or the radio on the frequency. She just needed to understand why the past still felt so present.
